title: From wanting to fight to wanting to know
hook: the Gita opens on armies wanting to fight, and turns when Arjuna asks to be taught
carry: jijnasa: the teaching begins when you ask to learn
tomorrow: who counts as 'my own people'? Arjuna asks.

segments.voice: Yesterday ended with the body's verbs and a lotus leaf: offer the deed; the ego is not the doer. Now the words go to work. The reading of the Gita's first chapter begins, back at its first line.

A blind king sits in his palace, far from the battle, and asks his advisor Sanjaya to tell him what's happening. That's how the Gita opens: not with God, not with a sermon, but with a worried father. On the field of the Kurus, he asks, gathered there, wanting to fight, my sons and the sons of Pandu: what did they do, Sanjaya? Wanting to fight is one word, yuyutsavah. Not fighting yet. Wanting to.
screen: `A BLIND KING ASKS.` → `MY SONS, AND PANDU'S.` → `YUYUTSAVAH: WANTING TO FIGHT.`

segments.voice: The line: dharmakshetre kurukshetre samaveta yuyutsavah, mamakah pandavash chaiva kim akurvata sanjaya. Yuyutsavah grows from yudh, to fight. Sanskrit can build a wanting-to form: the root's first sound doubles, and an s joins the end. Yudh becomes yuyuts-: wanting to fight. Now the same pattern somewhere very different. The Brahma Sutras, a root text of Vedanta, open: athato brahmajijnasa. Now, therefore, the wish to know Brahman. Jijnasa, from jna, to know: doubled sound, an s inside, wanting to know. And here's the teaching. The Gita itself travels from one wanting to the other. Through chapter one, Arjuna argues: reasons not to fight, reasons the war is wrong. Then, early in chapter two, he stops arguing and says to Krishna: I am your student. I have come to you; teach me. Shishyas te 'ham, shadhi mam tvam prapannam. Only then does Krishna begin to teach. That's how Hindu tradition says real learning starts: not with being right, but with the wish to know, and the humility to ask a teacher. It's the spirit in which students traditionally bow to the guru before a lesson, and Vedanta's first line is a wish rather than an answer. The field is full of people wanting to fight. The Gita happens because one man, for one moment, became a jijnasu, one who wants to know.
screen: `YUYUTSAVAH: WANTING TO FIGHT.` · `JIJNASA: WANTING TO KNOW.` · `I AM YOUR STUDENT. TEACH ME.` · `ONLY THEN DOES KRISHNA TEACH.` · then, large: `THE WISH TO KNOW COMES FIRST.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus begin study by touching the book with respect or saying a short prayer to the teacher. Try it: rest a hand on your heart, or on the book or screen in front of you, and say inside, teach me. If you don't pray, name one thing you honestly want to understand this week, someone else's side included, and breathe with that wish for the rest of the sit.
Reading the Gita's first chapter: today, yuyutsavah, wanting to fight, from yudh, and its cousin form jijnasa, wanting to know. Same pattern, two roads, and the Gita takes the second.
Your line: jijnasa, the teaching begins when you ask to learn. Arjuna stopped arguing and said, teach me. Chapter one, begun.

notes: Days 1475-1476 open the 'reading the Gita's first chapter' part; day 1477 (verse 1.2) follows. Day 1464 already taught mama/mamakah from 1.1 and days 1465-1466 used chaiva and kim akurvata, so this day's angle is yuyutsavah and the desiderative pattern, paired with jijnasa (Brahma Sutras 1.1.1).
Grammar: yuyutsu as the desiderative of yudh (reduplication + s), jijnasa as the desiderative of jna; the 'first sound doubles, an s joins' description is a plain-words simplification. Confirm.
Shape life: the hook starts from a family chat argument; the practice is a gratitude count plus one honest question.

Sanskrit is given in a simple romanization in the spoken text (no diacritics) so the voice can read it; the sources hold the same romanization. Confirm every word against a standard edition, and the verse numbers (editions differ by a verse around 1.27-1.28).
Grammar is described in plain words (endings, 'having done it', 'while doing it'); a Sanskritist should confirm each description.
